claims.claim: In Gen 7:1 the Hebrew text uses the divine name YHWH with the verb of divine address to Noah ("YHWH said to Noah"), and the event's text is about God's judgment on the earth — the name usage is part of the passage's texture.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 7:1 read directly via BibleGateway; 'the LORD said unto Noah' — the speaker is YHWH, and entry is grounded in Noah's righteousness 'before me in this generation.'

claims.claim: The Hebrew word *mabbûl* (מַבּוּל, H3999) is used only in Gen 6:17; 7:6, 7, 10, 17; 9:11, 15; 10:1, 32; 11:10 and Ps 29:10 — its ordinary sense is flood/deluge, its distribution is Genesis 6–11 plus one psalm, and the word is never used for an ordinary inundation.
claims.evidence: BDB H3999 read via BibleHub: 'flood in time of Noah'; derivation dubious; occurs only in Genesis + Ps 29:10, always absolute, usually articular.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:2 the Hebrew text distinguishes clean animals (*ṭāhôr*, H2889) from "the beast that is not clean" (*ʾašer lôʾ ṭᵉhōrâ* — a negated *ṭāhôr*, not the word *ṭāmēʾ*). The term *ṭāmēʾ* (H2930/H2931, "unclean") does NOT occur in Gen 7:1–8:19; the plan's lemma list entry for it must be corrected.
claims.evidence: BibleHub interlinear for Gen 7 read in full: 7:2 and 7:8 express 'not clean' by negated ṭāhôr; no H2930/H2931 token in Gen 7:1–8:19. BDB H2889: 'clean, pure.'

claims.claim: In Gen 7:2 the Hebrew *šibʿāh šibʿāh* ("by sevens") is a distributive expression: it gives seven pairs (or seven of each) for clean animals and fowl, versus two ("two and two") for the rest. The seven/two pattern is established; whether "seven" means seven pairs or seven individuals is disputed among commentators.
claims.evidence: Interlinear: šibʿāh šibʿāh (7:2–3) against šənayim šənayim (7:2, 7:8–9, 7:15). The distributive doubling does not by itself settle pairs vs. individuals; Keil & Delitzsch read seven pairs. The 7:8–9 summary 'two and two' covers even the clean animals — the tension is a real textual feature.

claims.claim: The seven-day notice in Gen 7:4 ("for yet seven days… I will cause it to rain") is a seven-day reprieve before the Flood begins, distinct from the 40 days of rain and the 150 days of prevailing waters.
claims.evidence: KJV Gen 7:4 read directly; fulfilled exactly on schedule at 7:10 ('after seven days, that the waters of the flood were upon the earth').

claims.claim: In Gen 7:11 the Hebrew *ʾărubbôt haššāmayim* ("windows of heaven") and *maʿyᵉnôt tᵉhôm rabbâ* ("fountains of the great deep") describe the Flood's two sources, heaven above and the deep below — a cosmic opening from both directions.
claims.evidence: Interlinear 7:11: maʿyənôt təhôm rabbâ (H4599 + H8415 + H7227) and ʾărubbôt haššāmayim (H699); both verbs Nifal — opened by divine action. Closed together at 8:2.

claims.claim: The word *tehôm* (תְּהוֹם, H8415) in Gen 7:11 is the same lexeme as in Gen 1:2, "the deep" over which the Spirit moved — the Flood narrative's vocabulary deliberately recalls the creation narrative.
claims.evidence: BDB H8415: sense (1) subterranean waters (Gen 7:11; 8:2) and sense (3) primeval ocean (Gen 1:2) are the same lexeme.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:16 the text says YHWH shut Noah in the ark; the Hebrew verb is *sāgar* (H5462, "shut/closed"). The shutting of the door is God's act, not Noah's.
claims.evidence: KJV 7:16 'and the LORD shut him in' — wayyisgōr YHWH baʿădô; the verse switches from 'God' (ʾĕlōhîm) in the command clause to YHWH for the shutting.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:17 the rain (*gešem*, H1653) fell "upon the earth" for 40 days and 40 nights; in Gen 7:12 the same 40-day figure appears. The 40 days is a distinct figure from the 150 days of prevailing waters in Gen 7:24.
claims.evidence: KJV 7:12 and 7:17 read directly; rain (haggešem, H1653) is distinguished from the two water-sources of 7:11.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:19 the Hebrew *wayyikassû* ("and were covered") — from *kāsâ* (H3680) — describes the waters covering the high mountains; the verb *kāsâ* is used for covering in the flood context and the verse's *kōl* ("all") is emphatic.
claims.evidence: BDB H3680 Pual (1): 'be covered,' mountains with water, Gen 7:19, 20. The covering is passive — the mountains are covered by the waters.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:20 the Hebrew says the waters "prevailed fifteen cubits upward" (*gābᵉrû hammayim*, from *gābar*, H1396) above the mountains. *Gābar* occurs four times in the Flood narrative (7:18, 19, 20, 24) and conveys overpowering might.
claims.evidence: BDB H1396 Qal (2) 'prevail,' absolute, of waters Gen 7:18, 19, 20, 24; 7:19 doubles məʾōd ('prevailed very, very much'). CORRECTION TO THE DOSSIER REGISTER: the register's parenthetical added 8:3, where the verb is ḥāsar (H2637), not gābar — removed per the dossier's own §4 lemma register, which lists gābar at 7:18, 19, 20, 24 only.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:21–23 the Hebrew *kōl-bāśār* ("all flesh," H1320 + H3605) is used for every living thing that died — the same phrase as in Gen 6:12–13, 17, 19 and 8:17; 9:11, 15–17. The phrase links the Flood's judgment and its covenant.
claims.evidence: BDB H1320/H3605: kol-bāśār = 'all flesh.' Same phrase denotes the animals entering (7:15–16), the creatures dying (7:21), and those exiting (8:17) — a deliberate inclusio.

claims.claim: In Gen 7:22 the Hebrew *nišmat-rûaḥ ḥayyîm* ("breath of the spirit of life," H5397 + H7307 + H2416) describes all that died on dry land — the phrase *nepeš ḥayyâ* (H5315 + H2416) does NOT occur in Gen 7:1–8:19. The plan's lemma list entry for *nepeš ḥayyâ* must be corrected: it is absent from this passage.
claims.evidence: Interlinear for Gen 7 and Gen 8 read in full: no H5315 token in either chapter. The passage's life-language is rûaḥ ḥayyîm (7:15), nišmat-rûaḥ ḥayyîm (7:22), kol-hayyâ (8:1, 8:17), and kol-bāśār.

claims.claim: The 40 days of rain (Gen 7:12, 17) fall within the 150 days of prevailing waters (Gen 7:24); the majority scholarly resolution treats the 150 days as the total period of the waters' prevailing, not a period following the 40 days.
claims.evidence: The dates force it: the 150 days run 2/17 → 7/17 (confirmed by 8:4), and the forty days of rain begin on 2/17. Hamilton, Genesis 1–17, 1:298, as quoted in a secondary study (Hamilton not read directly); Barrick & Sigler likewise (via search-result excerpt, not read directly).

claims.claim: In Gen 8:1 the Hebrew *wayyizkōr ʾĕlōhîm* ("and God remembered Noah") uses *zākhar* (H2142) with God as subject — a gracious divine action, not recall after forgetting. The same verb pattern (God remembering) occurs at Gen 19:29; 30:22; Ex 2:24.
claims.evidence: BDB H2142 II (God as subject): remember persons 'with kindness, granting requests, protecting, delivering' — citing Gen 8:1 and Gen 19:29. Sarna (via cited secondary) agrees: remembering is 'a focusing upon the object of memory that results in action.'

claims.claim: In Gen 8:1 the Hebrew *rûaḥ* (H7307) is used without the genitive "of God" — "God made a wind to pass over the earth." The echo of Gen 1:2 (*rûaḥ ʾĕlōhîm*, "Spirit of God") is a probable literary parallel; whether Gen 8:1's *rûaḥ* is the Spirit of God or an ordinary wind is disputed.
claims.evidence: BDB H7307: 8:1 is sense (2) wind; 7:15/22 are sense (1e) breath of life; Gen 1:2 is sense (9e). 8:1 has no 'of God' genitive, unlike 1:2, and the verb differs (Hifil of ʿābar vs. Piel of rāḥap).

claims.claim: In Gen 8:2 the Hebrew *wayyissākᵉrû* ("and were stopped") — from *sākar* (H5534) — describes the fountains of the deep and windows of heaven being closed; the verb is the reversal of the opening in Gen 7:11.
claims.evidence: Interlinear 8:2: wayyissākərû maʿyənôt təhôm waʾărubbôt haššāmayim (Nifal of sākhar, H5534); rain restrained (Nifal of kālāʾ, H3607). Exact reversal of 7:11–12; the opening/closing pair is morphologically matched (both Nifal).

claims.claim: In Gen 8:3 the Hebrew *wayyāšûbû hammayim* ("and the waters returned") — from *šûb* (H7725) — describes the waters receding from the earth; *šûb* is the hinge verb of the Flood's reversal, used in Gen 8:3, 7, 9, 12.
claims.evidence: BDB H7725 Qal: 'turn back, return'; with infinitive-absolute pairing, hālôk wāšôb (8:3) and yāṣôʾ wāšôb (8:7). Five tokens in the passage: 8:3 ×2, 8:7, 8:9, 8:12.

claims.claim: In Gen 8:4 the Hebrew says the ark "rested" (*wattānaḥ*, from *nûaḥ*, H5117) on the mountains of Ararat on the 17th day of the 7th month. The verb *nûaḥ* is the same root as Noah's name (*nōaḥ*) — a wordplay the narrative exploits.
claims.evidence: Interlinear 8:4: wattānaḥ hattēbâ baḥōdeš haššəbîʿî bəšibʿâ-ʿāśār yôm laḥōdeš ʿal hārê ʾărārāṭ. The resting is dated exactly five months (150 days on 30-day months) after 7:11.

claims.claim: In Gen 8:5 the Hebrew says the tops of the mountains were seen (*nîrʾû*, from *rāʾâ*, H7200) on the 1st day of the 10th month. The mountain tops' appearance marks the first visible sign of the waters' abatement.
claims.evidence: KJV 8:5 read directly: 'in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, were the tops of the mountains seen.'

claims.claim: In Gen 8:6 the Hebrew *ḥallôn* (H2474, "window") describes the opening Noah makes in the ark; it is a different word from *ṣōhar* (H6672, "roof/light") in Gen 6:16. Whether the window of Gen 8:6 is the same opening as the *ṣōhar* is uncertain.
claims.evidence: BDB H2474: 'open the window, Gen 8:6.' The text says Noah 'had made' this window — it is not in the building instructions of Gen 6. The text does not identify the two openings.

claims.claim: In Gen 8:7 the raven (*ʿōrēb*, H6158) is sent out first and "went forth to and fro" (*yāṣôʾ wāšôb*, from *yāṣāʾ*, H3318, and *šûb*, H7725) until the waters dried. The raven's going to and fro contrasts with the dove's returning.
claims.evidence: Interlinear 8:7: wayəṣēʾ yāṣôʾ wāšôb ʿad-yəbōšet hammayim. The text does NOT say the raven never returned; translations implying non-return go beyond the Hebrew. BDB H6158: raven, from 'grow dusky.'

claims.claim: In Gen 8:8–12 the dove (*yônâ*, H3123) is sent out three times at seven-day intervals; on the second return it brings "an olive leaf" (*ʿălê zayit*, H5929 + H2132) in its beak. The olive leaf is the first sign of new life after the Flood.
claims.evidence: BDB H3123: dove, Gen 8:8, 9, 10, 11, 12 (all J); hayyônâ, 'the dove' — articular, the same individual each time on the natural reading. 8:11: ʿălê-zayit ṭārāp̄ — 'a freshly-plucked olive leaf' (ṭārāp̄, H2965). Third sending (8:12): she did not return again.

claims.claim: In Gen 8:13 the Hebrew says the waters "were dried up" (*ḥārab*, H2717) from the earth in the 601st year, 1st month, 1st day. The verb is *ḥārab*, not *yābaš*; the plan's lemma list must be corrected on this point. *Yābaš* (H3001, "to be dry") occurs only in Gen 8:7 and 8:14.
claims.evidence: Interlinear 8:13: ḥārəbû — Qal of ḥārab (H2717); 'the face of the ground was dry' uses ḥārēb (same root). KJV renders both roots 'dried,' masking the change.

claims.claim: In Gen 8:14 the Hebrew says the earth "was dried" (*yābᵉšāh*, from *yābaš*, H3001) on the 27th day of the 2nd month of the 601st year. *Yābaš* is used of the earth's dryness here and of the waters' drying in Gen 8:7; the two uses frame the drying of the earth.
claims.evidence: BDB H3001 Qal (1c): 'of earth after the flood, Gen 8:14'; (2): 'be dried up: of water, Gen 8:7.' Two distinct dryness statements: 8:13 the waters dried / ground surface dry (ḥārab); 8:14 the earth was dry (yābaš). Whether they mark surface-dry vs. thoroughly-dry is probable at most, not lexically certain.

claims.claim: In Gen 8:15–19 God commands Noah to exit the ark with his family and the animals; the exit is by divine command, not Noah's initiative. The Hebrew verbs of going out (*yāṣāʾ*, H3318) echo the entry verbs of Gen 7.
claims.evidence: KJV 8:15–19 read directly; exit order mirrors entry order (Noah's household first, then animals by kinds). Noah does not leave on his own initiative even after seeing dry ground (8:13).

claims.claim: The Flood narrative's chronology, built strictly from the text, runs 370 days (exclusive count; 371 inclusive) from the 17th day of the 2nd month of Noah's 600th year to the 27th day of the 2nd month of his 601st year, on the 30-day-month assumption implied by the 150-day = 5-month equation (Gen 7:11, 7:24, 8:4); the total time aboard is 377 days (378 inclusive). No absolute date is assigned.
claims.evidence: Text arithmetic (§5): 2/17/600 → 2/27/601 = 12 months + 10 days = 370 days exclusive on 30-day months (371 inclusive); entry 7 days before the flood → 377 days aboard (378 inclusive). If months were lunar (~354-day year), the total would be ~364 days. The 30-day assumption is stated as an assumption, not a textual datum.

claims.claim: The Atrahasis epic (Old Babylonian, best-preserved copy from the reign of Ammi-saduqa, 17th c. BCE; scribe Ipiq-Aya; c. 1,245 lines) tells of a flood sent because human noise disturbed Enlil, who first tried plague, drought, and famine.
claims.evidence: Dalley, Atrahasis colophon as read (Tablet III, 390 lines; total 1,245); Lambert & Millard 1969 as standard edition (corroborated by CiNii bibliographic record). The motive is demographic/noise, not moral — no human wickedness is charged. Decisive contrast with Genesis.

claims.claim: In Atrahasis, Enki warns Atrahasis by speaking to the wall / reed hut of his house, evading an oath of silence, and gives a cover story for the elders.
claims.evidence: Dalley, Atrahasis III.i, as read: 'Wall, listen constantly to me! Reed hut, make sure you attend to all my words!' — with the cover story that Enki and Enlil have quarrelled.

claims.claim: In Atrahasis the boat is roofed "like the Apsu," has upper and lower decks, and is sealed with strong bitumen; its dimensions are NOT preserved in the surviving text.
claims.evidence: Dalley, Atrahasis III, as read: 'Roof it like the Apsu, so that the Sun cannot see inside it! Make upper decks and lower decks.' The dimension line falls in a gap in Dalley's translation; no figure (e.g. '150 cubits') was verified this session.

claims.claim: In Atrahasis the storm lasts seven days and seven nights; the landing and any bird episode fall in a ~58-line gap and are NOT preserved. Do not attribute a bird sequence or a landing mountain to Atrahasis.
claims.evidence: Dalley, Atrahasis III.iv, as read: 'For seven days and seven nights the torrent, storm and flood came on.' Then a gap of about 58 lines; Dalley's text resumes with the sacrifice.

claims.claim: In Atrahasis, after the flood the gods smell the sacrifice and "gathered like flies over the offering"; Enlil, furious that life escaped, imposes population controls (barren women, infant mortality, celibate priestesses) rather than a covenant.
claims.evidence: Dalley, Atrahasis III.iv–viii, as read: 'The gods smelt the fragrance, gathered like flies over the offering.' Enlil relents only by imposing population controls (ugbabtu, entu, egiṣitu priestess classes, the pašittu-demon). No covenant, no rainbow, no blessing, no immortality for Atrahasis.

claims.claim: In Gilgamesh Tablet XI the great gods decide to cause the Deluge; no motive is stated in Tablet XI itself. The noise motive belongs to Atrahasis and should not be imported into Gilgamesh.
claims.evidence: George, Tablet XI.14 (eBL), as read: 'The great gods decided to cause the Deluge.' No motive is stated in XI; the flood episode is widely held to have been taken over from Atrahasis (proposed, not established).

claims.claim: In Gilgamesh XI the boat is a cube: length = breadth, 1 *ikû* area, 120 cubits (10 rods) on a side, six decks / seven levels, nine compartments, sealed with bitumen and pitch.
claims.evidence: George, Tablet XI.28–31, 57–63 (ETANA), as read: 'one ikû was her area, ten rods the height of her sides… Six decks I gave her.' Contrast Genesis: a 300×50×30-cubit oblong, three decks.

claims.claim: In Gilgamesh XI the storm lasts six days and seven nights; the boat lodges on Mount Nimush; the bird sequence survives — dove returns, swallow returns, raven does not return (XI.145–154).
claims.evidence: George, Tablet XI.145–154, as quoted verbatim in two independent secondaries (cross-checked, same wording). Order: dove → swallow → raven (Genesis: raven first, then dove three times). Nimush was formerly read Nisir; location in the Zagros / vicinity of modern Sulaymaniyah is probable for the general region, uncertain for any exact peak.

claims.claim: In Gilgamesh XI, after the sacrifice the gods "collected like flies over a sacrifice"; Enlil blesses Utnapishtim and his wife with immortality and settles them "at the mouth of the rivers," far from humanity. There is no covenant with humanity.
claims.evidence: George, Tablet XI.156–162, as quoted: 'The gods smelled the savor, the gods smelled the sweet savor, and collected like flies over a sacrifice.' Enlil: 'Previously Uta-napishti was a human being, now he and his wife shall be like us gods.'

claims.claim: The Sumerian Flood Story (ETCSL t.1.7.4, "Eridu Genesis") survives in a single Old Babylonian tablet from Nippur, of which only about the lower third is preserved; it records a divine-assembly verdict to destroy "the seed of mankind" but no motive survives in the text.
claims.evidence: ETCSL t.1.7.4 translation read directly in full (Segments A–E, revision history to 2006-12-19). Single tablet CBS 10673, published by Poebel 1914 (via cited secondary); extant copy c. 1600 BCE (via cited secondary). Jacobsen coined 'Eridu Genesis' in 1981 (via cited secondary).

claims.claim: In the Sumerian Flood Story the storm lasts seven days and seven nights; there is no bird episode and no landing mountain named in the surviving text; Ziusudra sacrifices oxen and sheep to Utu, and An and Enlil grant him "life like a god" and settle him in Dilmun.
claims.evidence: ETCSL t.1.7.4, Segments D–E, as read: 'After the flood had swept over the land, and waves and windstorms had rocked the huge boat for seven days and seven nights, Utu the sun god came out.' 'Zi-ud-sura the king prostrated himself before Utu. The king sacrificed oxen and offered innumerable sheep.' No bird episode survives; no landing place is named.

claims.claim: The mechanism relating Genesis to the Mesopotamian flood traditions (direct borrowing, shared tradition, independent use of a common story-pattern) is disputed in scholarship and unknown on the evidence reviewed; the dossier does not settle it. The parallels are real and the contrasts systematic (moral judgement vs. noise; direct divine speech vs. oath-evasion; covenant vs. population controls or private immortality).
claims.evidence: Motif table (§7): parallels (warning through a wall, sealed multi-deck vessel, animals aboard, seven-day storm, birds, mountain landing, sacrifice the gods smell, furious Enlil) and contrasts (one God judging moral corruption vs. divided pantheon acting from irritation; direct speech vs. oath-evasion; covenant with all flesh vs. population controls or private immortality). Dependence vocabulary: established / proposed / unknown — no dependence claim is made.

claims.claim: The geographical extent of the Flood (universal/global vs. regional/local) is disputed: both readings have named scholarly defenders and textual arguments (*kōl*/*ʾereṣ* usage, "under the entire heaven," 15 cubits, duration, the ark's necessity, theological scope vs. relative uses of *kōl*, horizon language, the ark's landing near Mesopotamia, humanity's range). Neither reading is established by the evidence reviewed.
claims.evidence: §8: universal defenders Whitcomb/Morris (1961), Sarfati, Davis, Leupold, Waltke (as reported via cited secondaries); regional defenders Ramm, Young, Ross, Walton (2018) (as reported via cited secondaries). The universal language (kōl, 'under the entire heaven,' fifteen cubits) is emphatic in form; the same terms are used relatively elsewhere (e.g. Gen 41:57).

claims.claim: Mesopotamian flood deposits at Ur, Kish, and Shuruppak are real but asynchronous (Ur's deepest deposit is Ubaid; Kish's c. 2800–2600 BCE; Shuruppak's c. 2900 BCE), and Eridu shows no comparable layer; they do not establish a single synchronous flood, and the Shuruppak date c. 2900 BCE is not a date for the Genesis Flood.
claims.evidence: Roux, Ancient Iraq, via the Erenow-hosted text: the deposits occur at different stratigraphic levels at different sites, and nearby Eridu, excavated to virgin soil, shows no comparable flood layer. Woolley initially claimed his Ur layer was the biblical Flood; that claim is not established.

claims.claim: No site, layer, or geological feature is established as proof of the Flood; absence of proof is not proof of absence. Mainstream geology does not support a single recent global deluge as the primary agent shaping the Earth's crust; flood geology is a minority interpretive framework.
claims.evidence: §8: mainstream consensus as summarised in secondary sources explains sedimentary and fossil features through multiple events over deep time; flood geology (Whitcomb/Morris onwards) is an interpretive framework held by a minority of geologists. The dossier states the consensus and the dissent without presenting either as its own finding.

claims.claim: The Durupınar formation in eastern Turkey is a natural doubly-plunging syncline, not an authenticated ark: the 1996 Collins & Fasold study identified it as a folded sedimentary structure, and as of late 2026 no worked timber, joint, or structural element has been recovered and dated, and none of the recent (2022–2026) measurements has appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.
claims.evidence: Collins & Fasold 1996, 'Bogus Noah's Ark from Turkey Exposed as a Common Geologic Structure,' via cited secondaries (paper itself not read directly; volume/issue/pages unverified). Creationist geologists Snelling and John Morris reached the same geological conclusion. 2022–2026 revival (Ağrı İbrahim Çeçen University / Istanbul Technical University) via a single secondary (sacerdotus.com, Oct 2026); the team's own spokespeople have said they have not recovered an intact wooden ship.

claims.claim: Genesis 8:4 names "the mountains of Ararat" — a plural mountain region, the Hebrew form of Assyrian Urartu (kingdom centred on Lake Van) — not a single peak. The oldest landing traditions point to the Qardu/Corduene (Judi/Cudi) region; identification with the single cone now called Mount Ararat (Masis) is a medieval development.
claims.evidence: KJV 8:4 and interlinear: hārê ʾărārāṭ, plural 'mountains of Ararat.' BDB H780: Ararat is a district in Eastern Armenia; occurs 4× (Gen 8:4; 2 Kgs 19:37 = Isa 37:38; Jer 51:27). Jubilees names Lubar; Targum/Peshitta/Berossus/Syriac point to Qardu/Corduene (Judi/Cudi); the Masis identification is medieval (11th-century dating rests on a single secondary report — say 'medieval' only).

claims.claim: *Jubilees* 5:23–32 (Charles) retells the Flood with distinctive expansions: seven flood-gates of heaven and seven mouths of the fountains of the great deep, 40 days of rain, 15 cubits above the mountains, 150 days, and the ark resting "on the top of Lubar, one of the mountains of Ararat."
claims.evidence: Jubilees, Charles 1917, full text read via archive.org; Jub 5:23–32 read. Verse numbering for 5:24–26 varies by edition — cite as 5:24–25/26 with the variance flagged, pinned to the Charles edition.

claims.claim: *Jubilees* 6:17–22 makes the Noah covenant the charter for the annual Feast of Weeks and for four days of remembrance (new moons of the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th months); this is Jubilees' calendrical reception, not the biblical text.
claims.evidence: Jubilees, Charles 1917, 6:17–22 read: 'it is ordained and written on the heavenly tablets, that they should celebrate the feast of weeks in this month once a year, to renew the covenant every year.'

claims.claim: 1 Enoch 10:1–3 (Book of the Watchers) has the Most High send Uriel to warn Noah — "Hide thyself!" — mediating through an angel the warning Genesis gives directly from God to Noah.
claims.evidence: 1 Enoch, Charles 1917, ch. 10 read (sacred-texts.com): 'Go to Noah and tell him in my name "Hide thyself!" and reveal to him the end that is approaching.'

claims.claim: 1 Enoch 60; 65:1–69:1 (Book of Parables) contains Noah/Flood interpolations, probably from a lost "Book of Noah": Noah's cry to Enoch, the angels of punishment loosing the subterranean waters, God's assurance to Noah, and the naming of the fallen angels. The Parables have no Qumran fragments, and their dating and the interpolation identification are probable, not established.
claims.evidence: 1 Enoch, Charles/Schodde texts read via archive.org full texts + Reading Acts summary; ch. 65: Noah cries three times to Enoch; ch. 66: angels of punishment; ch. 67: God's assurance, 'the angels are making a wooden [ark]'. Exact wording of 67:2 varies by translation — established substance, uncertain wording. The Parables are the only part with no Qumran fragments (via cited secondary).

claims.claim: Josephus, *Antiquities* 1.3 (Whiston), retells the Flood for a Greco-Roman readership: a four-storey ark, Noah preaching before the Flood, the ark resting "on the top of a certain mountain in Armenia," the raven and dove, and the site called Apobaterion ("Place of Descent") where remains were still shown; he cites Berossus, Hieronymus, Mnaseas, and Nicolaus of Damascus as external witnesses.
claims.evidence: Josephus, Ant. 1.3.1–9 (§§73–108, Whiston) read in full: four stories (his gloss on Gen 6:16's three decks); Noah preaching (Genesis does not record it); raven first, then dove 'covered with mud' (his addition); 'The Armenians call this place Apobaterion.' External witnesses are Josephus's claims about other writers, not independent verification.

claims.claim: Josephus's flood date in *Antiquities* 1.3.3 is textually variant: the Whiston text gives "two thousand six hundred and fifty-six [one thousand six hundred and fifty-six] years from Adam" — which figure Josephus wrote is disputed.
claims.evidence: Whiston text read: 'two thousand six hundred and fifty-six [one thousand six hundred and fifty-six] years from Adam.' The bracketed figures are Whiston's textual variants; which figure Josephus wrote is disputed — do not present either as his settled figure.

claims.claim: Philo, *Questions and Answers on Genesis* II (Yonge), reads the ark allegorically as the human body (squared wood, nests as cavities, pitch as the soul's binding, 300×50×30 as bodily proportions) and the Flood as the deluge of the passions, while also affirming the literal construction. No standalone Philonic treatise *De Noe* was verified.
claims.evidence: Philo, QG II §§1–5, 25–36 read (Yonge, earlyjewishwritings.com); §13 via search snippet. QG II (1): the ark is 'the preparation of the human body.' QG II (30)–(33): the wind as 'the breath of the Deity'; QG II (31) reads the 27th day (against Genesis 8:4's 17th) — uncertain whether Philo's reading, a translator's error, or a textual variant.

claims.claim: 1 Peter 3:20–21 (KJV) is the New Testament typological key for the Flood: "eight souls were saved by water," and "the like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us." Justin Martyr (*Dialogue* 138), Tertullian (*De Baptismo* 8, "the baptism… of the world"), Cyprian (Ep. 75.2), and Firmilian (Ep. 74.15) develop it into the ark-as-Church typology: one ark, one Church, salvation by water, faith, and wood.
claims.evidence: KJV 1 Pet 3:20–21 read directly via BibleGateway. Justin, Dialogue 138 (ANF) read: eight as the eighth day, Noah as a figure of Christ, 'by water, faith, and wood.' Tertullian, De Baptismo 8 (ANF) read: 'after the waters of the deluge, by which the old iniquity was purged away — after the baptism, so to say, of the world.' Cyprian, Ep. 75.2, and Firmilian, Ep. 74.15 (ANF) read: 'the one ark of Noah was a type of the one Church.'

claims.claim: Augustine, *City of God* 15.26 (Dods), reads the ark as a figure of the Church rescued "by the wood on which hung the Mediator," taking over Philo's bodily-proportions reading of 300×50×30, the side door as the wound in Christ's side, and squared timbers as the steadiness of the saints; *City of God* 15.27 sets the both/and rule (history and allegory together). The 15.27 wording was not read directly.
claims.evidence: Augustine, City of God 15.26 (Dods) read directly: 'this is certainly a figure of the city of God sojourning in this world; that is to say, of the church.' 15.27 (both/and rule) and 15.14 (years then = years now) via cited secondary only — do not quote them.

claims.claim: Gordon Wenham's 1978 *Vetus Testamentum* article ("The Coherence of the Flood Narrative," VT 28.3: 336–348) reads Gen 6:10–9:19 as a 31-step palistrophe centred on Gen 8:1, "God remembered Noah," with the symmetrical day-pattern 7, 7, 40, 150, 150, 40, 7, 7. This is a scholarly reading, not textually certain; Emerton's critique is noted; Wenham's commentary (*Genesis 1–15*, WBC 1, 1987) was not read directly.
claims.evidence: Article not read directly; verified via two converging secondaries (From Dust to Glory; Constable's Expository Notes, quoting pp. 337, 339–40): 'a palistrophe containing 31 items... The turning point of the narrative is found in viii:1.' Wenham grants Noah's offering (8:20–21) falls outside the pattern and his observations do not rule out two sources. Emerton (1987/1988, via secondary summary) argues against the chiasmus on imperfections in the matching.

claims.claim: The source-critical division of the Flood narrative into J and P strands (Wellhausen; Friedman) is a disputed scholarly position; the counter-position (Wenham 1978; Andersen) reads the narrative as a coherent unity; the current state of the question is disputed, with the classical documentary hypothesis no longer held as Wellhausen stated it. The textual facts (differing animal numbers, 40 vs. 150 days, alternating divine names) are established; every explanation of them is disputed.
claims.evidence: Classical position (Wellhausen, Prolegomena 1878; Friedman, Who Wrote the Bible? 1987) via secondary summaries; counter-position Wenham 1978 + Andersen's syntactic argument (Gen 7:6–17 hangs together as one unit) via secondary; current state (Van Seters, Schmid, Rendtorff; 'the consensus around the classical documentary hypothesis has now faltered') via secondary. Keil & Delitzsch (Gen 7, read directly): the Jehovah/Elohim interchange 'furnish[es] no criterion by which to detect different documents.' Skinner (1910) reconstructs separate J and P Flood accounts (pp. 148–182) while treating the final form critically.

connections.note: The Flood carries out the judgement of Gen 6:5 ('the wickedness of man was great in the earth') and 6:11–13 ('the earth was filled with violence'). The two events are consecutive in narrative order (6 → 7) and share the mabbûl vocabulary. Strong. Cross-link both ways when both events are published.

Gen 8:20–9:17 (altar, covenant, rainbow, blessing) is the direct sequel: the Flood ends in Gen 8:19, the covenant begins in Gen 8:20. The Flood event's text should point forward to it without duplicating its claims. Strong.

'For this is as the waters of Noah unto me: for as I have sworn that the waters of Noah should no more go over the earth; so have I sworn that I would not be wroth with thee, nor rebuke thee.' Isaiah names the Flood 'the waters of Noah' and cites God's oath never again to flood the earth — the covenantal reading of the Flood in the prophets. Strong.
'But as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.' The Flood becomes the type of sudden, unrecognised judgement. Strong.
'By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house.' Hebrews names Noah's ark-building as an act of faith. Strong.

'Which sometime were disobedient, when once the longsuffering of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was a preparing, wherein few, that is, eight souls were saved by water.' The New Testament's own typological key. Strong — the central NT link.

'And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly.' 'Preacher of righteousness' is a New Testament characterisation of Noah — not a Genesis fact — and the Flood event must present it as such. Moderate.

'For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water: whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished.' Quote 3:5–6 together for context; present as a theological reading, never as a geographical proof. Moderate–strong.
